entries.title: Commanders Come Up a Few Yards Short in Week 1 Loss to Eagles
entries.content:
The Commanders' revamped defense held the fort for most of Sunday afternoon in Philadelphia. The unit limited Saquon Barkley on the ground and put pressure on Jalen Hurts. For the most part — the key word being most — Washington kept Philadelphia at bay at Lincoln Financial Field. But it took just four plays to undo all of that progress.

The defense allowed a 64-yard bomb to Dontayvion Wicks in the first quarter, leading to the game's first touchdown. It gave up a 42-yard run by Barkley, setting up Philadelphia's second score. Then there was the 22-yard scramble by Hurts on a key 3rd and 18 late, leading to the biggest dagger of them all: a 43-yard touchdown pass to Dallas Goedert that proved to be the difference.

Behind those big plays, the Eagles took the season-opener, 24-22, after the Commanders failed on a two-point conversion with just over a minute left in the fourth quarter.
https://x.com/NFL/status/2099280633705152539The Washington offense was mostly anemic on the afternoon, failing to reach 40 yards of total offense in the first quarter. But they came alive when it mattered most in the fourth. Stefon Diggs scored on a 10-yard touchdown pass from Daniels, and a series later rookie Antonio Williams made a fingertip touchdown grab at the goal line to bring the Commanders within two. But a failed shovel pass to tight end John Bates on the two-point conversion sealed the Commanders fate.

Daniels finished 18 of 34 for 164 yards and two touchdowns.


The defense sacked Hurts three times, had 10 tackles for loss and put together a strong overall showing. But Philadelphia's chunk plays and the offense's slow start proved too much to overcome.

entries.title: Trump Is Spending in Every Senate Battleground but One
entries.summary: The president’s new political committee dropped millions across four new Senate races last week, but Trump’s spending is still quiet in Maine.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump reported his largest spend so far this weekend, sending $21 million to candidates in competitive races as pressure ramps up for Republicans two months before the midterms.



The president’s Senate spending before Sept. 8 had largely concentrated on Republican nominee Ken Paxton in Texas, with his $10 million drop coming after party leaders urged him to get more involved. A set of financial disclosures filed Sept. 10-12 show Trump recently backed four additional battleground Senate candidates at the end of last week — while still ignoring incumbent Sen. Susan Collins’ toss-up race in Maine.



No Going Back PAC Inc. — a new committee formed Sept. 1 under Trump’s super PAC, MAGA Inc. — spent roughly $6.7 million in Ohio, $3.7 million in Michigan, $1.7 million in New Hampshire and $779,000 in Georgia, concentrated on TV-ad buys and mailers opposing the Democrats in those races.



Trump’s disbursements come as Senate Majority Leader John Thune’s new Texas PAC reported its first $6.6 million investment in the state’s Senate race on Sunday, with a combination of media and text-service buys in support of Paxton and against Democrat James Talarico. The group, associated with Thune’s Senate Leadership Fund super PAC, also reportedly booked more than $51 million in advertising Friday to help Paxton.



As the dust settles from a flurry of disclosures in the first two weeks of September, Thune’s political committee has now entered every major battleground Senate race, while Trump has yet to report dropping significant money in Maine.



Trump and Collins have had a complicated relationship, though he publicly voiced support for the senator’s reelection in June and called her a “sane person” even if “she’s not my best friend at all.” But the five-term senator has recently tried to distance herself from some of Trump’s most unpopular policies for her state, like the president’s ongoing trade war with Canada and a fatal shooting involving a federal immigration agent in July.



The president is going to soon embark on a national tour of in-person campaign stops and telerallies after hosting a midterm convention in Dallas last week, though some Republicans are still worried that Trump entered the spending spree too late in the game.



No Going Back also made expenditures in a new set of House races, including putting roughly $492,000 against Democrat Jamie Ager in North Carolina, $422,000 against Democrat Lindsay James in Iowa, $274,000 against Democratic Rep. Vicente Gonzalez in Texas, $109,500 against Democratic Rep. Greg Landsman in Ohio and $65,000 against Democrat Sam Forstag in Montana.

entries.title: NFL Week 1 Takeaways: The Bears Might Be a Juggernaut
entries.summary: The first Sunday of the season featured a comeback in Houston and an upset in Los Angeles.
entries.content:
After appetizers on Wednesday and Thursday, NFL fans got a full meal Sunday afternoon with the first real slate of games. And there was plenty to enjoy, from Josh Allen’s heroics to a throwback performance from Kirk Cousins. Here are five takeaways from Week 1:

The Bears’ offense might be a juggernaut

In his first year in Chicago, Ben Johnson led the Bears to an 11–6 record and their deepest playoff run since 2010. But he set the bar even higher ahead of this season. In addition to chasing a Super Bowl, Johnson has openly talked about having the “highest-scoring offense ever.”

“I want shutouts,” Johnson told The Athletic. “I want blowouts.”

Johnson got his blowout Sunday, as the Bears beat up on the Panthers, 59-37. Two years ago, Chicago didn’t score their 59th point until Week 4. But Caleb Williams was a rookie then, and in his first game of Year 3, he looked to be in full control of the offense. Williams went 21 for 29 for 269 yards and two touchdowns and rushed for two more. D’Andre Swift added 124 yards and three touchdowns on the ground as the Bears totaled 552 yards of offense.

Chicago’s 59 points set a franchise record for highest output in a season opener and tied for second-most points by any team in a Week 1 game.

The NFC favorites had a rough opening week.

Two Super Bowl hopefuls started their seasons off with key injuries. On Wednesday, the defending champion Seahawks lost quarterback Sam Darnold to a glute injury in the first quarter of their Super Bowl rematch against the Patriots. While the Seahawks still pulled out a 13-10 win behind backup Drew Lock, they could be without Darnold for a “couple of games,” according to NFL Network.

The Rams, who went all in on their Super Bowl hopes by trading for Myles Garrett this offseason, also took a hit this week. After falling flat against San Francisco in Thursday’s Australia game, the Rams announced that Garrett will undergo arthroscopic surgery on his knee and miss at least four games on injured reserve. Garrett, the reigning defensive player of the year, played a full game against the 49ers but didn’t register a tackle or sack.

“This was the worst version of myself that I’ve put out there, and I’ve got to be better,” Garrett said after the loss. “I’ve got to find a way to recover and get back to the player I know I can be and I’ve shown that I’ve been before.”

Joe Brady AP - 26256659737363 (5616x3744, AR: 1.50)
A few new coaches earned impressive first wins. 

In his first game as coach of the Bills, Joe Brady was tasked with putting together a game-winning drive. Buffalo’s former offensive coordinator, who was elevated to head coach this offseason while maintaining play-calling duties, put his faith in quarterback Josh Allen with the Bills down 31-30 in the fourth quarter. Allen led the Bills on a seven-play, 96-yard scoring drive to take a late, 36-31 lead. Texans quarterback C.J. Stroud nearly mimicked that feat, leading the Texans down to the Bills’ 18-yard line with 25 seconds left. But a strip sack from Greg Rousseau ended the game and gave Brady’s Bill their first win.

Meanwhile, the Ravens traveled to Indianapolis and made a statement in their first game under coach Jesse Minter. Derrick Henry ran for 144 yards and three touchdowns in a 41-23 blowout. Mike McCarthy led the Steelers to a 20-13 win over the Falcons and Las Vegas’ Klint Kubiak earned a 27-13 win against the Dolphins.

Don’t forget about the old QBs. 

It’s been quite a two-year stretch for Kirk Cousins. In March 2024, he signed a four-year, $180 million contract with the Falcons, only to watch Atlanta draft a first-round quarterback a month later. That rookie, Michael Penix, eventually unseated Cousins as the starter in Atlanta. This offseason, Cousins signed with the Raiders knowing the team would draft Indiana quarterback Fernando Mendoza first overall in April’s draft.

Even if he has accepted the role of mentor, Cousins showed on Sunday that he can still produce as a starter. The 38-year-old completed 21 of 30 passes for 160 yards and three touchdowns in a 27–13 win over Miami. He became the first Raiders starter to throw three touchdowns in the season opener since Kerry Collins in 2005.

But Captain Kirk wasn’t the only starter who showed he still has some juice: 33-year-old Jacoby Brissett went 27 for 37 for 277 yards and a touchdown as the Cardinals opened the season with a surprising 26–14 win over the Chargers in Los Angeles.

entries.title: Trump Officials Are Selling an Economy Americans Aren’t Buying. Sound Familiar?
entries.summary: “There is a pretty strong parallel between the way the Biden administration handled the question of inflation,” one expert said.
entries.content:
The midterm elections are getting closer, and the Trump administration’s explanations for rising inflation are getting further from what many voters and independent economists are describing.

Trump’s economic policy advisers have zeroed in on indicators like wages, GDP and stock market growth to sell Americans on a humming economy. Americans are reporting a different experience. In a July Pew Research Center poll, 60% of U.S. adults said that President Donald Trump’s second-term policies have made the economy worse.

The dissonance has reminded former Biden officials of a dynamic they caution can be a losing battle: trying to explain the economy to American voters.

“During the Biden administration, there was a genuine disconnect between improving macroeconomic indicators and how households experience the cumulative increase in their day-to-day prices,” said Tonantzin Carmona, who served as Biden’s special assistant for economic policy on the National Economic Council.

The economic conditions are different now than when Biden was president. Trump is presiding over a ballooning stock market, while Biden was tasked with jump-starting a sputtering pandemic economy with record-high unemployment. The former president’s policies stoked inflation to highs that Trump hasn’t been able to tamp back down, despite the economic growth driven by the AI industry.

That’s led economists to question the White House’s continued focus on positive indicators that don’t reflect workers’ struggles with high inflation.

After sweeping back into power by castigating President Joe Biden for being out of touch with the average American’s pocketbook, Trump and Republicans are experiencing the other side of their own messaging playbook.

“There is a pretty strong parallel between the way the Biden administration handled the question of inflation,” said William Galston, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution. “In neither case were the respective administrations in touch with what people were thinking, feeling, experiencing on the ground in their daily lives.”

Trump’s economic agenda has made for a challenging political environment ahead of the midterms.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said a recent Treasury analysis found that if companies passed the total costs of U.S.-Canada tariffs on to consumers, there would be a near-zero effect on inflation. The countries are locked in a trade war, with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney rolling out tariffs on $20 billion worth of U.S. goods and Trump outright banning many Canadian imports.

“So the pain to the U.S. — there is none,” Bessent said Tuesday at a Breitbart News event.

The Treasury Department did not respond to multiple requests for the report Bessent cited.

Researchers at the Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis found that tariffs contributed 0.2 to 0.4 percentage points to core inflation, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, as of July. Year-over-year core inflation punched in at 3.3% that month.

Economists at the St. Louis Federal Reserve Bank found that tariffs in fact account for a lesser share of inflation in recent months, but that’s likely because soaring energy prices are driving inflation numbers up.

Bessent’s remarks are the latest example of the Trump administration characterizing the economy differently than how people are feeling it. On Tuesday, Bessent touted rising wages, particularly for workers without college degrees and those in the bottom quartile of income earners.

High school-educated workers may be experiencing good times, but on the whole, the nation’s rising wages aren’t keeping up with inflation, meaning workers have less purchasing power than they once did.

“Inflation is a little bit higher than we would like, but — this is important — coming down,” Christopher Phelan, Trump’s chief economic adviser, said Tuesday at the Breitbart event. Inflation increased by 0.4% in August, according to a Bureau of Labor Statistics report released Friday.

Sameera Fazili, the former deputy director of Biden’s National Economic Council, said Bessent’s comments reflect the challenge administration officials face in spinning good news from poor economic conditions.

“When you’re a communicator communicating the policy, you always want to have hard numbers to back the talking point that the political offices are asking you to deliver,” Fazili said. “What voters are upset about is the price level that they are experiencing right now, and instead he is trying to find some talking point on inflation and future price increases.”

Former Biden administration officials say the Trump administration is repeating their mistakes, with a key difference: They argue Trump’s inflation woes are self-inflicted, related to his tariff policies and the Iran war, compared to Biden’s pandemic-era problems.

“The distinction today, though, is that some of the Trump administration policies can themselves add to the affordability pressures people are describing,” Carmona, who’s currently the director of economic policy at the left-leaning Century Foundation, added.

The Iran war has added more than $100 billion in extra costs to Americans’ energy bills as of this week, according to an estimate by Brown University’s Climate Solutions Lab. Soaring energy costs trickle down to production and transit expenses for food, apparel and other necessities, as tariffs also raise prices for certain common goods.

Several Republicans in tight races have criticized Trump’s trade agenda, citing economic concerns. Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine), who’s in one of the most competitive races of the midterm cycle, has come out against the president’s trade war with Canada. So has John Sununu, the Republican Senate contender in New Hampshire, as The Washington Sun previously reported.

Democratic Senate candidates in Michigan, Ohio and Alaska, looking to retake the Senate majority, have hammered their Republican opponents on trade.

“Consumer confidence is lower than it has ever been. That means it's lower than when we had 9% inflation in 2022,” said Neera Tanden, who served as Biden’s domestic policy adviser. “I think that is a product of the fact that costs and wages are out of whack for basically the bottom 60 to 70% of workers.”

“The greatest irony to me is there is no president that I'm aware of who has adopted a series of policies that raise costs and create additional burdens for working-class people,” added Tanden, who is currently the president and CEO of the left-leaning Center for American Progress.

The president himself has acknowledged that his policies have created price pressures but has argued that the temporary economic pain is worth it to achieve bigger goals, such as eliminating a nuclear threat from Iran or reshoring American manufacturing.

"Guys come up, 'You know, I wish you didn't do the war in Iran. Gasoline's up,'" Trump said in his speech at the Republican midterm convention on Wednesday. "And I say ... let me ask you one question: Can Iran have a nuclear weapon? 'Absolutely not.' Well then, I'm right, then I win."

White House spokesperson Kush Desai defended the impact of Trump’s policies on the economy in a statement to The Washington Sun.

“Last year, President Trump increased America’s average tariff rate by nearly sevenfold yet inflation cooled,” Desai said. “While President Trump had always been clear about temporary disruptions as a result of Operation Epic Fury, the August CPI report showing dramatic month-over-month declines in beef, prescription drug, and auto insurance costs is proof that the Administration’s policies continue to deliver long-term economic relief for the American people.”

“That's the argument you make when you've run out of economic arguments,” said Lindsay Owens, the president and CEO of the left-leaning Groundwork Collaborative. “You saber-rattle about foreign adversaries, and you wax poetic about a bygone period of American manufacturing.”

entries.title: What to Know About D.C. Council Member Trayon White’s Bribery Trial
entries.summary: Including a surprising approach to White’s defense.
entries.content:
Opening statements could begin as early as this week in the criminal trial of Ward 8 council member Trayon White, who stands accused of pocketing money from a D.C. contractor in exchange for attempting to steer city contracts in his favor.

It’s a trial with high personal stakes for White, who faces potential prison time if convicted — and high political stakes for the entire District.

White has represented the city’s poorest ward on the council since 2017. A ubiquitous community presence and self-described advocate for those left behind in traditional politics, the lawmaker has clung to a political career despite his legal troubles. He was expelled by his council colleagues following his 2024 criminal indictment, but he returned to the dais last year after winning less than a third of votes in a crowded, low-turnout special election to fill the vacant Ward 8 seat.

Now, his two-year legal saga will culminate in federal court, where in the coming days government prosecutors will present their case against White, and he will get the chance to defend himself.

Here’s what you need to know.

What is White accused of?

Prosecutors allege that White repeatedly accepted money in exchange for promising to help a prolific D.C. government contractor secure continued business with the city, particularly in the area of violence interruption services.

The charges, laid out in a 30-page indictment, largely stem from a series of alleged meetings between White and a confidential informant, later identified as Allieu Kamara. Kamara was cooperating with authorities after pleading guilty to separate bribery and fraud charges, and the FBI surreptitiously recorded his meetings with White during the summer of 2024.

Kamara handed White $35,000 in cash over the course of those meetings, according to prosecutors. In exchange for the cash, prosecutors allege, White agreed to help Kamara maintain his government contracts, and the two discussed White getting kickbacks from Kamara’s future contract earnings, to the tune of more than $100,000.
Trayon White (5173x3449, AR: 1.50)White allegedly told Kamara that he was working to help him, meeting with various government officials at D.C.’s Office of Neighborhood Safety and Engagement and D.C.’s Department of Youth Rehabilitation Services about renewing Kamara’s various grants.

In the meetings, White also allegedly discussed future potential arrangements with Kamara involving contracts in the mental health space. “That shit a cash cow,” he told the informant, according to prosecutors.

What can we expect from White’s defense?

Last month, White’s defense attorneys did something interesting: They told the federal judge overseeing the trial that they wouldn’t contest the government’s allegations that White had taken and kept the cash from Kamara. (The exchanges were caught on video, so fighting them would have been a challenge.)

But what they will be fighting is prosecutors’ claims that the money actually constituted a bribe. And for that, the case of former Virginia Gov. Bob McDonnell will be particularly helpful.

In 2014, McDonnell was convicted of charges related to him and his wife accepting $135,000 in gifts, loans, trips and other goods from a Virginia businessman. Two years later, though, the U.S. Supreme Court unanimously overturned McDonnell’s conviction, saying that the government had not proven that he’d taken official action in exchange for the gifts.

“The Supreme Court has narrowed the bribery statute and there’s got to be a quid pro quo,” said Erica Hashimoto, the director of the appellate litigation program at the Georgetown University Center.

Prosecutors have said White actively contacted and spoke with government officials on Kamara’s behalf, pushing them on the status of his contracts. But his defense team has directly challenged that claim.

“If the defendant did no more than seek information on the status of the informant’s contracts, he has not violated … the bribery statute,” the defense wrote in proposed jury instructions.

They also raised another possible defense: The money Kamara gave White wasn’t a bribe, but rather a legal gift of goodwill between friends.

A legal concept called entrapment could also factor into the trial. White’s attorneys have started preparing a claim that the FBI essentially set him up and induced him to commit a crime he would not have otherwise, writing in proposed jury instructions: “Mr. White asserts that he was entrapped by the government to commit the crime of bribery.”

Do White’s arguments stand a chance?

Peter Zeidenberg, a former public corruption prosecutor in D.C. who is now a partner at ArentFox Schiff, said that the Supreme Court’s ruling in the McDonnell case has made it more difficult to convict elected officials on bribery charges. But he added that the footage of White accepting the cash could be hard to overcome for the jury.

“When you have cash changing hands and it was videotaped, from a defense perspective, you’ve got a very difficult situation with a jury,” he said. “It doesn’t smell right. Nobody looks at that situation and thinks, ‘This is normal.’ A public official should not be getting cash from a constituent. What is he doing it for? It is a very problematic set of facts from a defense perspective.”

On the entrapment argument, Hashimoto says the claim could be buttressed by the fact that Kamara was working as a confidential informant for the FBI at the time that he allegedly bribed White.

“It does look like the government went after White and set him up, essentially, and jurors don’t always like that,” she said.

Still, claiming entrapment as a defense raises its own new risks, Zeidenberg said.

“That would put a burden on the defense to establish that the government overwhelmed his will by enticing him to do something he would not otherwise have done,” he said. “That opens up the door to other acts that might be admissible to show you’re a bad guy, you’ve done things like this before. That can be problematic.”

Who will testify?

The government anticipates it will call Kamara, the informant around which the case is built, as a witness. Several high-ranking D.C. officials are also expected to testify, including Lindsey Appiah, the deputy mayor for public safety and justice, and Kwelli Sneed, director of the Office of Neighborhood Safety and Engagement.

White’s defense anticipates calling several witnesses to testify on the council member’s character, including his former council chief of staff Wanda Lockridge.

What happens if he’s convicted?

White faces up to 15 years in prison if convicted. If found guilty, he will also immediately become ineligible for public office in D.C., and Ward 8 residents will elect a new lawmaker to represent them.

What happens if he’s acquitted?

If White is acquitted, his colleagues on the council will face the politically thorny question of whether to expel him again.

When lawmakers first voted to expel White, they said they could not abide by what they saw as clear evidence of serious misconduct. But they took heat from some civic leaders in Ward 8, who accused them of upending the will of voters before the justice system had its final say.

In the backdrop, of course, is also the Trump administration, which has been eager to flex its authority over the nation’s capital. Some political observers in D.C. fear that Trump or Congress may use White’s continued presence on the council to justify further federal intervention in local affairs.

How long is the trial expected to last?

In pretrial filings, prosecutors said they anticipate taking about five days to present their case against White. White’s attorneys say his defense will probably take one or two days. Then the jury will deliberate.

entries.title: Commanders Come Up a Few Yards Short in Week 1 Loss to Eagles
entries.content:
PHILADELPHIA — The Commanders defense held down the fort in Philadelphia — for the most part.

They limited running back Saquon Barkley on the ground for the most part. They got in the face of quarterback Jalen Hurts for the most part. Everyone from the defensive line to the defensive backs played with physicality for the most part.

Washington’s defense looked far better than it did for most of 2025. But four big plays undid all of that progress.

The unit allowed a 64-yard bomb to Dontayvion Wicks in the first quarter, leading to the game’s first touchdown. It gave up a 42-yard run by Barkley, setting up Philadelphia’s second score. Then there was the 22-yard scramble by Hurts on a key 3rd and 18 late, leading to the biggest dagger of them all: a 43-yard touchdown pass to Dallas Goedert that proved to be the difference.

Behind those big plays, the Eagles took the season opener, 24-22, after the Commanders failed on a two-point conversion with just over a minute left in the fourth quarter.

https://x.com/NFL/status/2099280633705152539Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

Aside from the 42-yarder, Barkley averaged just 2.6 yards per carry. Hurts was sacked three times and faced near constant pressure as the Commanders forced five three-and-outs on the day. But each of his three touchdown passes came from breakdowns on the defense. While Washington put the hurt (no pun intended) on the Eagles Sunday, including 10 tackles for loss, it was missed tackles that often did them in.

“It's always a couple plays that deter the game from what it really looks like to how it ended,” defensive tackle Tim Settle said. “[The mistakes] were self-inflicted. The more we can work on beating the team instead of beating ourselves, we'll be completely pumped.”

The Washington offense was mostly anemic early, failing to reach 40 yards of total offense in the first quarter. But the unit came alive when it mattered most. In the fourth quarter, Stefon Diggs scored on a 10-yard touchdown pass and rookie Antonio Williams made a fingertip grab in the end zone to bring the Commanders within two in the game’s final moments. But a failed shovel pass to tight end Jon Bates on the two-point conversion sealed the Commanders fate.

“I would say we stopped shooting ourselves in the foot,” Daniels said of the offense’s turnaround. “Especially against a really good defense like that … you don’t want to play at third-and-longs and let that crowd and that defense feast and rally to the ball. We shot ourselves in the foot too many times and came back to haunt us at the end of the game.”

Game MVP: Antonio Williams

Not bad, rook. The first-year receiver from Clemson led Washington's pass-catchers with 64 yards and tied for the lead in receptions (four). His touchdown with 1:05 left in the fourth quarter gave the Commanders a chance to tie the game.

Earlier in the afternoon, he caught a slant route for 16 yards, putting Washington on the 1-yard line just before halftime. Bill Croskey-Merritt punched it in on the next play for the Commanders’ first touchdown of the season.

In the fourth quarter, he caught a 33-yard pass on 3rd and 14, keeping a drive alive and leading to Diggs’ touchdown three plays later.

“I just want to build that confidence,” Williams said. “And when it comes to me I'm going to make the most of it.”

Moment that mattered

The moment that seemed to start the snowball effect of mental mistakes was the 64-yarder to Wicks. Mike Sainristil was in coverage on the deep throw, and it appeared he lost track of the ball as it soared over his head. Not only did the play lead to Philadelphia’s first touchdown, it seemed to throw Sainristil off for the rest of the half. Two possessions later, he lost track of Wicks again — this time in the end zone.


After the game, Sainristil said he let up on the deep pass because he incorrectly thought the ball had already been thrown in front of him. He turned to find the pass-catcher, not realizing it was Wicks.


https://x.com/NFLonFOX/status/2099240337474486427
Postgame scene

Even though it was a frustrating loss for Washington, the away locker room didn’t have the despondent vibe close losses tend to create. Sainristil talked shop with cornerbacks Rasul Douglas and Amik Robertson, discussing how to improve. Few, if any players, denied requests for interviews. Everyone on defense seemed to understand that, outside of a few isolated mistakes, they played a solid game. But, of course, there are no moral victories in football.

“We lost, so we’re all losers right now,” Douglas said. “We just gotta work, practice and put on tape next week.”

entries.title: Trayon on Trial
entries.content:
Good morning. This is The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for Sept. 14, 2026. You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free!

In today’s newsletter: The Trayon White trial, a warning about D.C.’s economy and the Commanders’ season-opening defeat.

THE LATEST

A particularly high-stakes moment in D.C. politics is set to play out in the coming weeks, but it won’t be in City Hall — it will be in a federal courthouse.

Opening statements in the federal bribery trial of Ward 8 council member Trayon White could begin as early as this week. The long-awaited trial comes more than two years after he was indicted on charges of taking $35,000 in cash from D.C. businessman Allieu Kamara in exchange for promises that he would help Kamara maintain his existing contracts and land new ones.

White has conceded that he accepted the money. But as The Washington Sun’s Jenny Gathright and Martin Austermuhle report, his defense attorneys are expected to argue that he didn’t actually do anything official in exchange to help Kamara. A decade-old Supreme Court ruling involving former Virginia Gov. Bob McDonnell may help White — it tightened the definition of what it takes to prove that an elected official was actually bribed.

But those envelopes full of cash that were handed to White — all caught on video — will probably hang in the minds of jurors, said Peter Zeidenberg, a former public corruption prosecutor in D.C. who is now a partner at ArentFox Schiff: “It doesn’t smell right. Nobody looks at that situation and thinks, ‘This is normal.’”

The role of the FBI may also come into play. White has claimed he was entrapped by the government, and the fact that Kamara was working as an informant for the FBI may help buttress the claim. “It does look like the government went after White and set him up, essentially, and jurors don’t always like that,” said Erica Hashimoto, the director of the appellate litigation program at Georgetown Law.

White’s legal problems have hung over the city since he was indicted, and his trial comes as the Trump administration and congressional Republicans have aggressively inserted themselves into the city’s local affairs. Should he be convicted, White could face prison time — and would be immediately expelled from the council, triggering a special election in Ward 8.





DEEP DIVE

D.C. Chief Financial Officer Glen Lee isn’t mincing words. 

In a presentation to the D.C. Chamber of Commerce last week, Lee told an audience of local business leaders that "economic and revenue signals are flashing red."

More than 36,000 jobs have been lost since June 2025, largely from federal government layoffs. The unemployment rate in D.C. stood at 6% in June, above the national rate of 4.3%. The office vacancy rate is up, and business tax revenue is down.

One positive note is that revenue from individual income taxes is up. But that comes with a caveat: Most of that is from people doing well in the stock market, or residents who received severance payments from the federal government. Lee said the revenue is “wild and subject to sudden swings,” unlike the preferred streams from property and sales taxes.

Lee’s warnings seemed to have had their intended effect. One attendee tells The Sun that the crowd came out of the event “sobered” about the challenges ahead.

Those challenges include a growing deficit that D.C. lawmakers will have to close next year — just as Janeese Lewis George, the expected winner of November’s mayoral race, will be trying to enact her ambitious agenda. In October, the council will start discussing possible tax increases to bring in more revenue, but there’s no certainty yet that they’ll actually pass any into law.

Lee’s warnings aren’t gospel: Some of his critics say that while they don’t contest that D.C. is facing economic headwinds, the CFO has sometimes underestimated how much revenue the city takes in. Earlier this summer, D.C. Auditor Kathy Patterson criticized Lee’s relationship with the council and urged him to more fully explain his dire predictions. “The CFO is damaging his office’s credibility by sounding alarms without adequate explanation,” she wrote.





FROM THE DISTRICT

Reflecting Pool AP - 26249769200328 (5575x3717, AR: 1.50)
Contractors admitted that their own errors, not vandalism, caused damage to the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, The Sun’s Gavin J. Quinton reports. New documents show that Atlantic Industrial Coatings said workers had mistakenly layered two incompatible materials that caused paint on the pool liner to peel — and the government had knowledge of this error as it pursued criminal vandalism charges earlier this year.

Kennedy Center leaders say the venue is on the brink of bankruptcy and could close as soon as Tuesday, The Washington Post reports. In documents distributed to the center’s board, officials say the only way to avoid “certain fiscal collapse” could be putting President Donald Trump’s name on the building and therefore ensuring his support. Officials also recommend closing the building until a renovation is complete. The board could approve such a move at a special meeting Tuesday.

Trump wants a massive statue of George Washington installed outside the National Museum of American History. In a post to Truth Social last week, Trump wrote that he would like to see the "Infinity" sculpture that has stood outside the museum since 1967 replaced by a 30-foot statue of the founding father. Trump also proposed a five-year exhibit on Washington, starting in 2027 and running to his 300th birthday in February 2032.

WMATA has amended a policy requiring all bus operators to quote fares to passengers after public backlash over potential driver safety issues, WJLA reports. Now, only drivers in “fully enclosed workstations” are required to remind passengers of the fare. WMATA says it’s investing $18 million to install fully enclosed workstations on all buses by next May.





FROM MARYLAND

We Are CASA, a national immigrant rights advocacy group, filed a lawsuit last week against the Department of Homeland Security on behalf of four Maryland residents over what they say are unlawful arrests by ICE agents, The Sun’s Kendall Staton reports.





D.C. TRIVIA

Which group’s song inspired the name of legendary D.C. punk band Bad Brains?

  1. The Clash
  2. The Ramones
  3. The Rolling Stones
Email us your answer — the first reader who gets it right will receive a shout-out at the end of tomorrow’s newsletter.




SPORTS

Jayden Daniels Eagles AP - 26256835961582 (4787x3191, AR: 1.50)
Eagles 24, Commanders 22: After stumbling through a 5-12 campaign last year, Washington showed signs of improvement in Sunday’s season opener. A revamped defense held the Eagles mostly in check, but Jayden Daniels and the offense took some time to get going. When they did, new additions Stefon Diggs and Antonio Williams scored second-half touchdowns and the Commanders gave themselves a chance to tie the game late. That hope ended with a failed two-point conversion attempt.

We’ve got you covered after a dramatic Week 1:

  • Martenzie Johnson breaks down the game and its key moments.

  • And Alex Schiffer rounds up the biggest Sunday storylines from the rest of the league.

entries.title: Congress vs. The Machines
entries.content:
Today’s notice: Congress returns to perhaps, maybe address AI. Sen. Mark Kelly hits the campaign trail. Sen. Marsha Blackburn’s non-gubernatorial campaign fundraising. What’s next for “Pod Save America”? And: the Trumps’ crypto moves. 

THE LATEST

Congress returns to Washington today to face reality on artificial intelligence. The snowballing worry from outside critics, inside developers and AI CEOs appears to put the issue on an emergency, red-alert level for lawmakers to do something to avoid the threat of rogue agents. There’s nothing like the head of Anthropic warning of the risks of cyberattacks, bioterrorism and serious economic disruption to spur Congress into action, right?

Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vermont) plans to convene his colleagues Wednesday for a briefing on the "extraordinary dangers” of AI. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries said AI will be a high priority for Democrats in their weekly caucus huddle. So, yes, you can expect a lot of talk from Washington about AI.

“We have to resist Congress jumping in and imposing some sort of emergency moratorium. It's got to be done right, safely, wisely," House Speaker Mike Johnson told CNN’s “State of the Union.”

Donald Trump, too, said yesterday he doesn’t want to curtail AI development, especially in the race against China, because “whoever wins AI wins.” (Oh, and he told reporters on Air Force One that he uses AI but not how he uses it: “I don’t want to tell you that.”)

Keep an eye out this week for remarks from two top industry executives who say it’s time to “pace the frontier.” Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman speak Tuesday at Salesforce’s tech forum. Trump’s former AI czar David Sacks, who’s put the onus on the companies to rein this in, is also speaking at Politico’s Decoded Summit.

With 50 days until the midterms, expect this issue to ratchet up with voters, just like data centers are now squarely in the campaign sights. Barack Obama said recently that Democrats should map out how the party will tame AI’s risks should they retake the majority, The New York Times reported, and he pushed prospective 2028 candidates to make it a central campaign issue.

Given Congress’ penchant for can-kicking, we asked Claude, in its own estimation, will Congress take action on AI? “My honest guess: incremental, sector-specific stuff limps forward; the comprehensive framework gets kicked to 2027 regardless of who controls Congress,” Claude told us. OK, then.

More: Trump Says He Doesn’t Care if Voters See this Election as a Referendum on Him • Johnson Says Trump Needs ‘Congress to Act’ on His $5,000 Checks • Wisconsin Congressman Tearfully Recounts Surviving Emergency Plane Landing • What to Know About D.C. Council Member Trayon White’s Bribery Trial

FROM THE CAMPAIGN TRAIL


Sen. Mark Kelly’s road trip: The Arizona Democrat, who is not yet running for president, will travel to Michigan and South Carolina next month to campaign for his party’s candidates, and that’s on top of stumping in 15 states in the last year. “All of us need to be out there and do whatever we possibly can to help candidates get across the finish line,” Kelly told The Washington Sun’s Alex Roarty.

The aggressive campaign schedule nonetheless serves a dual purpose, Alex writes, helping Democrats this year while signaling to potential donors, activists and voters that the senator can effectively campaign in red states and districts, winning over the kinds of voters any Democratic presidential nominee would need in a general election. Kelly said he’ll consider a presidential bid after the midterms.

“These emails won’t stop until we get an answer.” Those are the type of incessant fundraising missives, many replete with false urgency and high pressure, sent by Sen. Marsha Blackburn’s campaign, which has raised more than $9 million so far this cycle. But the Tennessee Republican isn’t running for reelection, she’s vying for governor — and federal contributions can’t be directly used for state-based campaigns.

But some of that money is still wending its way toward her gubernatorial campaign, The Sun’s Dave Levinthal reports. Federal and state campaign finance records indicate the senator’s federal joint fundraising committee, the Blackburn Tennessee Victory Fund, is helping seed a network of conservative Club for Growth super PACs with millions of dollars. And one of the network’s PACs is now spending millions of dollars to boost Blackburn’s gubernatorial campaign.

FROM THE WHITE HOUSE


The challenge in selling the economy: Former Biden officials told The Sun’s Jade Lozada that Trump is experiencing some of the same challenges on economic messaging that plagued his predecessor. Tonantzin Carmona, who served as Joe Biden’s special assistant for economic policy on the National Economic Council, said there was a “genuine disconnect” between improving economic indicators under Biden and Americans’ continued experience with rising prices.

Trump and his market messengers, like Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, are “trying to find some talking point on inflation and future price increases,” while what voters are more “upset about is the price level that they are experiencing right now,” said Sameera Fazili, the former deputy director of Biden’s National Economic Council.

THE BIG ONE 

What is “Pod Save America” up to? What was once a mainstream, often milquetoast liberal media platform that was criticized for being too beholden to the ever-amorphous party “establishment” now reflects the party’s existential woes, The Sun’s Emily Kennard writes.

With the 2028 cycle looming, the podcast now plays host to the fights inside the Democratic Party that could help define the forthcoming primary. The hosts’ positions within the ongoing intraparty war are hard to pin down, Emily writes, though former Obama adviser Tommy Vietor tells her, “I don't know that the current DNC leadership is the biggest fan of our show.”

The establishment wing isn’t such a big fan, either. “I've watched lots of ‘Pod Save’ where they're critiquing the current Democratic Party and the Democratic establishment, and I just think: ‘Didn't you help construct this for eight consecutive years?’” said Third Way’s Yemisi Egbewole.





NEW ON THE WASHINGTON SUN

Cashing out on crypto? Trump and his three sons are taking steps that would allow them to cash out the digital “tokens” created by their family’s crypto firm, The Sun’s Jeff Stein scoops. While the change in holdings does not definitely mean that they are looking to sell their tokens, the new contract kicks off a two-year waiting period — and a lot of concerns around conflict of interest, too.

“It has never been clear what World Liberty Financial was supposed to do other than enrich the Trumps, and here we have them taking the first avenue they can to offload their coins,” Zach Everson, research director at Public Citizen, told Jeff.

A lawyer representing the Trump firm World Liberty Financial told Jeff that the “premise of your questions is misguided,” and a spokesperson said “there are no imminent sales.”

entries.title: Mark Kelly Campaigns in Red States, for This Election And Maybe the Next
entries.summary: In an interview, the Arizona senator and potential 2028 presidential candidate said he thinks his working-class roots help him connect with Republican voters.
entries.content:
Democratic Sen. Mark Kelly will campaign in Michigan and South Carolina next month, according to an aide, visits to early presidential primary states that are certain to stir speculation about his future.

For the senator, however, the stopovers are part of a broader effort to help Democrats ahead of November’s midterm election — especially in red districts and states that aren’t always welcoming to national Democratic politicians.

Since last year, Kelly has visited 15 states to boost Democratic candidates, meeting voters, rallying with volunteers and raising money to help the party win House and Senate seats. The campaign stopovers have been concentrated in purple and red states, including North Carolina, Georgia, Ohio, Iowa and Kansas, each of which is home to a competitive Senate race.

In October, Kelly will visit another purple state, Michigan, to campaign with Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed, and a red state, South Carolina, to help Democratic Senate nominee Annie Andrews.

In an interview with The Washington Sun, Kelly reiterated that he would consider a potential presidential run after November but, for now, he is focused on this year’s election.

But the aggressive campaign schedule nonetheless serves a dual purpose, helping Democrats this year while signaling to potential donors, activists and voters that the senator can effectively campaign in even red states and districts, winning over the kinds of voters any Democratic presidential nominee would need in a general election.

“All of us need to be out there and do whatever we possibly can to help candidates get across the finish line,” Kelly said. “Some of these races are going to be really close, but we have an opportunity to win in some unexpected places.”

Kelly visited another early presidential state on Saturday, walking in the Navajo Nation Parade in New Mexico, before campaigning in his own state of Arizona.

Aides say that Kelly has also raised or contributed more than $10 million for Democratic candidates or party committees this election cycle, including over $3.5 million to the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee and $2 million to the Democratic National Committee. And in August, the senator raised more than $350,000 for Sherrod Brown, the Democratic Senate nominee in Ohio, after a three-day tour of the state.

Kelly, who has twice won the swing state of Arizona, said he’s able to campaign in deep Republican turf in part because of his blue-collar background. Both his parents were police officers.

“I didn’t go to some fancy Ivy League school,” he said. “I went to the U.S. Merchant Marine Academy, where, along with a degree in engineering, I learned how to weld and start up a boiler, and worked in hot and sweaty engine rooms. I think I have a background that resonates with a lot of working-class people.”

“I went into the Navy, but my dad wasn’t like an admiral in the Navy, right? I didn’t have a trust fund. I just worked my way up.”

Kelly demurred when asked why Iowa, where he campaigned last month with Democratic Senate nominee Josh Turek, has trended away from Democrats.

“I haven’t been doing this a long time. I’m sure somebody wrote a paper in some political science class on it,” the senator said. “I think these things often go in cycles in different places and people are frustrated and when they don't feel like the government is delivering for them and making smart choices for them and their families, they go in a different direction.”

Kelly is one of many Democrats eyeing a presidential run who have actively tried to help Democrats win races this year, in what strategists say is an early attempt to woo the party before the primary starts in earnest next year. Former Vice President Kamala Harris is set to campaign in some electoral battlegrounds, including Georgia next month, while Illinois Gov. J.B. Pritzker announced a new political action committee this week that would spend $20 million on midterm races.

Former Department of Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, meanwhile, has traveled extensively this year, making public appearances in roughly 30 states on behalf of nearly 50 candidates. He, like Kelly, has also campaigned in some deeply red areas, and this past weekend campaigned in a battleground House district in Arizona.

“It’s a signal to both voters and the opinion-makers that this is someone who can appeal to red-state swing voters,” said Addisu Demissie, who managed Cory Booker’s 2020 presidential campaign and has also worked with Democrats including California Gov. Gavin Newsom, who recently campaigned for Democrats in South Carolina. “And that has traditionally been an important criteria that Democratic primary voters evaluate their presidential candidates on.”

Kelly already has some credibility in that area, Demissie added, given his swing-state success. He also has more than $20 million banked in his own federal campaign account, money that could immediately seed a presidential bid should he decide to run.

The senator, whose public fight with Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth has helped raise his national profile, told The Sun that he would make a decision about running for president on his own timeline and not be pressured into making a quick decision after November.

“It's full speed ahead until November,” Kelly said. “On the other side of that, at some appropriate point, I don't know exactly when that is, but I'll make a decision, whether or not … I feel it's the right thing for, first, the country, and then for my family, to pursue higher office.”

entries.title: Is the Trump Family Preparing to Cash Out on Its Own Crypto?
entries.summary: President Donald Trump and his three sons have taken a step that would permit them to sell World Liberty Financial’s digital tokens.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump and his three sons have taken a step that would permit them to cash out the digital “tokens” created by the family’s cryptocurrency firm, intensifying concerns from ethics experts about potential conflicts of interest.

On May 19, four anonymous digital wallets simultaneously moved more than 20 billion in $WLFI — one of the two crypto “tokens” launched by the Trumps’ firm — to a vesting contract. The new contract kicks off a waiting period after which the accounts are able to sell their holdings.

One of the exchanges was for the precise amount of crypto that Trump was awarded when setting up the firm, World Liberty Financial, which he controls. Three of the others match precisely the amount of crypto given to other relatives of the president. Trump’s sons — Don Jr., Eric, and Barron — are the only other family members who have been identified as founders.

The change to the holdings has not been previously reported. In a statement to The Washington Sun, Eric Hageman, a partner at a law firm representing World Liberty Financial, said that new governance rules approved by the company required its founders to move the tokens to a vesting contract and denied that the new vesting contract represented a first step toward a sale of the tokens.

“The premise of your questions is misguided,” Hageman said. “WLFI token holders approved a governance proposal that obligated the founders to burn 10 percent of their holdings.”

However, three experts who reviewed World Liberty Financial’s governance documents told The Washington Sun that the transaction was optional, and government watchdogs are concerned the Trump family is taking steps to get a payout.

“It has never been clear what World Liberty Financial was supposed to do other than enrich the Trumps, and here we have them taking the first avenue they can to offload their coins,” said Zach Everson, the research director at Public Citizen.

David Wachsman, a spokesman for World Liberty Financial, emphasized that there was still a two-year vesting period before the tokens could be sold. "You must note that co-founder’s tokens are unable to be sold for a very long time," Wachsman said. "There are no imminent sales."

World Liberty Financial brands itself as a "next-generation financial platform" that will improve the speed and efficiency of sending money between platforms. Government watchdogs have long warned that it could instead amount to a legal way for foreign investors and domestic consumers to curry favor with the Trump family by purchasing a “token” currency of little real value.

While their value would decline if sold, the tokens owned by the family are currently valued at more than $1 billion. The president has already reported more than $550 million in income from sale of World Liberty Financial tokens, while retail investors have lost $1 billion from their investments in the company, according to an analysis by a blockchain company.

Hageman said the founders were obligated to remove 10% of their $WLFI holdings from circulation, and that “the only way” to do so was to move them into a vesting contract. Wachsman also said that "all" the co-founders of the company agreed to the "overwhelmingly popular governance proposal."

The company's latest governance rules, approved on May 6, state that founders "will have the option to elect less favorable unlock terms or remain locked indefinitely." Before the transfers, the crypto tokens were considered “locked” and could not be moved. After the transfers, the tokens can be sold after a vesting period.

Additionally, the governance document states the conditions of the vesting contract apply "if" founders "opt in." It adds that if a founder "does not affirmatively accept this new vesting schedule, their tokens will not be burned and they will continue to have their tokens locked indefinitely." The tokens can be used to vote on World Liberty Financial’s governance.

"They could've stuck with the indefinite lock," said Molly White, a crypto expert who runs a newsletter covering cryptocurrency, technology, and tech policy. “They say explicitly in the WLFI proposal that was voted in that it was optional … The Trump family is laying the groundwork to cash out their WLFI stake.”

Trump’s personal allotment of 14.175 billion in $WLFI tokens has a current market value of roughly $1 billion, though that would surely plummet if the president tried to sell them. The other three accounts, appearing to belong to Trump’s sons, each contain roughly 2.75 billion in $WLFI tokens, which would likely be worth hundreds of millions of dollars in the event of a sale.

The opportunity to use Trump’s crypto firm to buy influence with the White House has raised alarms. Chinese crypto billionaire Justin Sun bought $75 million in $WLFI tokens, after which the Securities and Exchange Commission dismissed an outstanding civil fraud lawsuit against Sun and his businesses. Four days before Trump’s inauguration, a firm backed by top officials in the United Arab Emirates also purchased a 49% stake in the family crypto firm.

The White House has previously said Trump has "no involvement in business deals that would implicate his constitutional responsibilities.”

Hageman and Wachsman did not respond to requests for comment explaining the diverging interpretations of the company’s governance documents.

“It’s right there in the documents: It’s an option. The terms of the deal make it clear that the big insider holders have the option to choose which investment path their tokens go down,” said Corey Frayer, who served as senior adviser to former SEC chair Gary Gensler, who is now the director of investor protection for Consumer Federation of America. “Within that set of options, one of them is to exit out. And it looks like they’re trying to turn their monopoly money into something that is real.”

entries.title: The Commanders’ Dilemma: Protect Jayden Daniels or Let Him Loose?
entries.summary: In Week 1, Washington’s young quarterback stuck to a new script until his team needed a hero.
entries.content:
PHILADELPHIA — Jayden Daniels walked through the bowels of Lincoln Financial Field and toward the Washington Commanders’ bus Sunday night with every limb fully intact and operable, if not downright pristine. For a quarterback who spent most of 2025 either unable to get on the field or unable to stay there, that represented progress.

“It’s been a long time [Dec. 7, 2025, to be exact] since I played football,” Daniels said after the Commanders’ season-opening 24-22 loss to the Philadelphia Eagles. “A long time since I started and finished a game.”

In a perfect world, the Commanders wouldn’t have to choose between keeping their franchise quarterback healthy and winning games. In a perfect world — such as the one they inhabited in 2024, when Daniels was a spectacular rookie and the Commanders were a 12-5 juggernaut — they can accomplish both objectives.

But here, at the start of the 2026 season, it’s already feeling like something close to a binary choice. And for most of Sunday night’s entertaining game, it felt like the Commanders were unsure which side of that line they wanted to occupy.

Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

They absolutely, positively, 100% don’t want Daniels to feel like he has to go out there and win games for them with his unique blend of athleticism, artistry and aerial acumen. Until they absolutely, positively, 100% need him to do exactly that. And then, it seems, they are willing to hold their breath and turn him loose.

On Sunday night, that strategy almost won them a crucial game in a stadium that has long been a house of horrors for this franchise. But it fell two points short when the final play of the game — a two-point-conversion try featuring an ill-conceived shovel pass to tight end John Bates — was stopped shy of the goal line.

Almost everything the Commanders did in the offseason seemed designed with one purpose in mind: keeping Daniels upright for 17 games. Behind rookie coordinator David Blough, they installed an offense full of motion and deception, with Daniels largely coming out of the huddle and playing under center — as opposed to the old, up-tempo design with Daniels mostly in the shotgun formation. They surrounded Daniels with the best collection of offensive weapons and targets of his pro career. They emphasized quick, smart decisions that boiled down to one notion: You don’t have to be the hero.

For the first three quarters Sunday night, the Commanders mostly stuck to that script. And what did that get them? A 17-9 deficit. Nine completions in 24 attempts for Daniels, for a total of 65 passing yards. No sacks, but no touchdown passes. Their longest play from scrimmage at that point was for 15 yards. They were 2 for 11 on third-down conversions. Terry McLaurin, their two-time Pro Bowl wideout, had two targets and no catches.

Daniels, though, was doing a bang-up job of not being the hero.

Asked afterward if it was beginning to feel natural for him to play smarter and safer, Daniels said, “It’s natural. I mean, kind of. But yeah, it’s natural. [The goal is] protecting the team, and when a play is there to be made with me scrambling, using my legs to go out there and make a play. But when there’s nothing there, don’t try to force anything. ... Throw the ball away. I’m kind of proud of myself for that.”

But with the final play of the third quarter, everything suddenly changed. Now operating out of the shotgun, Daniels saw the pocket collapse, shifted to his right, then took off downfield. He spun around one would-be tackler, then another — as you could practically hear the Commanders’ coaches yelling, “No, no, no, no, YES!” — and wound up with a 13-yard gain and a first down.

https://x.com/NFL/status/2099270551802151394
It was vintage Daniels, circa 2024, and it seemed to stir something in him. He suddenly got a little less risk-averse, taking his first sack of the day later in that drive. But he also stood in the pocket, against what is likely to be the best defense he will face all season, and unleashed a 33-yard laser to rookie Antonio Williams, then three plays later found veteran Stefon Diggs in the end zone for a touchdown.

“You see how we have success when we sustain drives,” McLaurin said. “Staying out of second and long, third and long, and converting in situations where we had to, and staying on the field.”

By the time Daniels, trailing now by eight late in the fourth quarter, moved the Commanders down the field for a late touchdown — finding Williams in the end zone from one yard out with just over a minute left — it seemed obvious what they would do with the two-point conversion try. Don’t overthink it. Let your best player — who happens to be the one through whom every play must run — make a play.

Instead, they ran the shovel pass to Bates, a run-blocking specialist of a tight end. Center Nick Allegretti missed his block, and Bates came up well short of the goal line.

“I knew the play. It was a good one,” coach Dan Quinn said of Blough’s play-call. (A Commanders spokesperson said Blough was unavailable to speak Sunday, but would address the media during his regularly scheduled appearance on Thursday.) “It just didn’t execute, which sucks.”

Things get no easier from here for the Commanders. They travel to Dallas next week, then make their home debut in Week 3 against the defending Super Bowl champion Seattle Seahawks — part of a stretch in which they play against five 2025 playoff teams in their first eight games.

These next couple of months would have looked a lot less daunting with a win here against the Eagles. And a win here against the Eagles would have been a lot more feasible had Daniels turned himself loose a quarter or two sooner.

The heart wants Daniels to go out there, make plays and win games the way he did in 2024. The head wants him to be smart and stay on the field all season, the way he did not in 2025. Maybe it’s too much to ask that Daniels, in 2026, can do both.

entries.title: Blackburn Is Raising Millions for a Federal Race While She Runs in a State One
entries.summary: Some of the funds from her federal joint fundraising committee are making their way toward her gubernatorial bid.
entries.content:
“INACCURACY DETECTED”

“CORRECTION REQUIRED”

“Your MAGA Loyalty File shows incorrect information”

“These emails won’t stop until we get an answer”

For months, Sen. Marsha Blackburn’s federal political operation has sent prospective donors incessant fundraising missives, many replete with false urgency and high pressure — tactics criticized by government agencies and elder advocacy groups. Sometimes, emails arrive multiple times a day.

They work: The Tennessee Republican’s operation has raised more than $9 million during the 2026 election cycle, according to Federal Election Commission records. Much of that money comes from tens of thousands of small-dollar contributions sent by individual donors who’ve responded to solicitations, records indicate.

Blackburn isn’t running for reelection to a federal office. She’s campaigning for state office — governor of Tennessee — where federal campaign dollars generally can’t get spent.

But some of that money is still wending its way toward her gubernatorial campaign. Federal and state campaign finance records indicate the senator’s federal joint fundraising committee, the Blackburn Tennessee Victory Fund, is helping seed a network of conservative Club for Growth super PACs with millions of dollars. And one of the network’s PACs is now spending millions of dollars to boost Blackburn’s gubernatorial campaign.

Blackburn’s novel financial machinations have alarmed some political ethics watchdogs, who say they blur lines between different campaigns and could skirt the spirit, if not the letter, of rules governing the intermingling of state and federal political cash.

“It raises red flags,” said Stuart McPhail, director of campaign finance litigation at Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, which generally supports stronger campaign finance laws. “It’s fair to ask, ‘Why is a state-level candidate using a federal committee in this way?’”

Blackburn’s Senate office directed questions to Blackburn’s gubernatorial campaign, which did not respond to repeated requests for comment. The Club for Growth and several of its connected super PACs did not respond to inquiries.

Blackburn’s multi-step transfer of political wealth to Club for Growth’s political committee network began last year with the Blackburn Tennessee Victory Fund, which is composed of her Senate campaign, federal leadership PAC and a federal arm of the Tennessee Republican Party:

  • The Blackburn Tennessee Victory Fund shifted about $2.1 million to Marsha for Senate, Blackburn’s dormant Senate campaign committee over the course of 15 months, from March 2025 to June 2026.
  • Marsha for Senate contributed $4.8 million to the Club for Growth Action super PAC on May 8, as first reported by the Tennessee Lookout.
  • Club for Growth Action contributed $3.55 million to School Freedom Fund Oklahoma, an affiliated state-level political committee established in April, between May 11 and June 8.
  • The School Freedom Fund — a related political committee funded by billionaire businessman Jeff Yass, and which shares a Washington, D.C., address with the School Freedom Fund Oklahoma — contributed $4.81 million to the Tennessee Freedom Fund between May 7 and July 7.
  • The Tennessee Freedom Fund spent nearly $1.8 million between June 10 and July 9 to advocate for Blackburn’s gubernatorial campaign.
State and federal campaign finance records covering the groups’ activity during August and September aren’t slated for public release until next month.

Bradley Smith, a former Republican chairman of the Federal Election Commission, said the Blackburn Tennessee Victory Fund is legally permitted to continue raising money, particularly since Blackburn hasn’t categorically ruled out running for Senate in the future. (Her current term expires in early 2031.)

The Blackburn Tennessee Victory Fund and Marsha for Senate committees can legally contribute money to super PACs, which may then independently choose how to use that money, including in state races, Smith added.

Tennessee state law prohibits a federal campaign committee from transferring funds to a state-level committee maintained by the same candidate, but does not address the kind of financial moves the Blackburn Tennessee Victory Fund has made.

“There are good reasons to keep raising money for the federal committee,” said Smith, who’s now chairman of the Institute for Free Speech, which generally opposes strong campaign finance laws.

The bipartisan FEC would typically investigate any complaint accusing the Blackburn Tennessee Victory Fund, or any federal committee, of not complying with federal campaign finance rules.

But the commission has been almost entirely out of commission since May 1, 2025, when it lost its legally required quorum of four commissioners needed to execute high-level business, such as formalizing investigations, conducting audits, interpreting statutes, penalizing scofflaws and even conducting public meetings.

President Donald Trump, who alone may float new commissioners to fill empty seats, waited until February to float the Senate two nominees for confirmation. Since then, the Senate has failed to even conduct a confirmation hearing for the pair of Republicans, Ashley Stow and Andrew Woodson.

The FEC declined to comment.

“This underscores how we need a functioning FEC to investigate these questions,” said Faith Williams, senior policy manager for anti-corruption and accountability at Common Cause. “The Senate can do something about it — wouldn’t that be nice — but isn’t.”

Recent polls show Blackburn with a sizable lead over her main gubernatorial race rival, Democrat Jerri Green. The Republican entered August with about $2.7 million in her state campaign account. Green’s campaign, in contrast, had about $118,000.

Meanwhile, back at the federal level, the Blackburn Tennessee Victory Fund keeps asking potential donors for money with aggressive pitches:

“I reached the point I hoped we’d never hit”

“Notice of Rescindment”

“RESPOND ASAP TO CONFIRM YOUR MAGA CLEARANCE!”

entries.title: DMV High School Football Players of Week 3
entries.summary: This weekend’s standouts included a two-way playmaker from South Lakes and a hyper-efficient running back from B-CC.
entries.content:
Week 3 of the high school football season featured a full slate and several high-profile matchups. Here are five players that turned in exceptional performances in their teams’ wins:

Joshua-Benjamin Dagbe, Junior, Defensive Back, South Lakes

Dagbe was one of the brightest stars in South Lakes’ momentous 34-12 win over Virginia Class 6 power Battlefield on Thursday. The defensive back, who also plays wide receiver for the Seahawks, nabbed an early interception and returned it 48 yards to the house to give Coach Jason Hescock’s team some early momentum. Dagbe then pulled down two touchdown catches on offense and racked up 160 scrimmage yards as South Lakes stunned the Bobcats. Through three games, Dagbe has seven total touchdowns and two interceptions.

Gabe Hudgens, Senior, Wide Receiver, Theodore Roosevelt

The senior wideout has already started building a strong resume for DCIAA Player of the Year. In a thrilling comeback victory over Digital Pioneers Academy on Friday, Hudgens tallied 172 receiving yards and two touchdowns as the Roughriders stormed back from an early 16-point deficit to earn a 29-28 victory. “I don’t see many teams that can stop him one-on-one,” Coach Chris Harden said of Hudgens. “I think teams are going to have to put two or three guys on Gabe, because Gabe is a monster out there on that field.”

Akeem Jervis, Senior, Quarterback, Largo

Jervis torched Glen Burnie in more ways than one in Largo’s 50-34 win last week. The senior rushed for 132 yards and a touchdown and threw for 123 yards and two more scores as the Lions poured it on against a Glen Burnie team that advanced to the Maryland 4A state quarterfinals last season. Coach Derron Thomas’ run-heavy offense finished with 336 rushing yards.

Aiah Mbayo, Senior, Running Back, Bethesda-Chevy Chase

Mbayo produced a handful of explosive plays to help key Bethesda Chevy-Chase’s 50-36 victory over Blair on Thursday. The senior made the most of his eight carries, running for 152 yards and two touchdowns on the ground. He added a third touchdown with a 98-yard kickoff return as the Barons brushed off last week’s gut-wrenching loss to rival Churchill with a huge offensive showing.

PJ Sutherland, Senior, Running Back, Westfield

Sutherland found the end zone three times in the Bulldogs’ 35-28 win over Langley on Friday. His first came in the first half, when he hauled in a deep pass over his shoulder for a 56-yard receiving touchdown to give Westfield a two-score lead. Sutherland’s second touchdown was equally impressive — with his team clinging to a one-score lead deep in the second half, he burst through a horde of Saxon tacklers for a 10-yard touchdown run. His final score, a 23-yard jaunt to the end zone with just minutes left in the fourth quarter, gave the undefeated Bulldogs a nice cushion.
